description: Validation, least privilege, secret handling, and the everyday habits of writing code that fails safely.

screens.body:
Every value from outside your code is suspect until checked: form fields, URL params, API bodies, file uploads — even data from your own database if users wrote it.

Client-side validation (in the browser) is UX — it gives fast feedback. But attackers bypass the browser entirely, so the real check must live on the server.

Check type, length, format, and range. "An age of -5 or 999 is nonsense" is a security check, not just tidiness.

options: On the server — browsers can be bypassed
check.question: Where must validation happen to actually protect you?

screens.heading: Validate everything, trust nothing
screens.keyPoint: Browser validation is UX. Server validation is security.

screens.body:
Give every user, service, and database account the minimum power it needs — nothing more. A reporting tool gets read-only access, not admin.

Why: when (not if) something is compromised, least privilege shrinks the blast radius. A stolen read-only key reads; a stolen admin key destroys.

Apply it to your code too: don't run your app as a superuser, and don't hand every user the admin role "just in case".

check.question: A reporting tool only reads data. What access should it get?

screens.heading: Least privilege: the smallest key that works
screens.keyPoint: Minimum power needed. Shrink the blast radius.

screens.body:
API keys, passwords, tokens — secrets never belong in source code. Code gets copied, screenshotted, pushed to GitHub, and shared.

Keep secrets in environment variables or a secret manager, and load them at runtime. Add .env files to .gitignore so they never get committed.

If a secret leaks (it happens), rotate it immediately: revoke the old one, issue a new one, and check logs for misuse.

options: An environment variable or secret manager
Hardcoded at the top of app.js
check.question: Where should an API key live?

code.snippet:
// GOOD: secret arrives at runtime, never in the repo
const apiKey = process.env.PAYMENTS_API_KEY;

screens.heading: Secrets don't live in code
screens.keyPoint: Secrets live in env vars, never in code.

screens.body:
Error messages help developers — and attackers. A stack trace, or "user not found" vs "wrong password", tells an attacker exactly how your system works and which accounts exist.

Show users a generic message: "Something went wrong." Log the full details server-side, where only your team sees them.

Think of it like a bouncer: polite "not tonight" to strangers, full incident report to the manager.

options: "Invalid email or password" (same message either way)
check.question: A login fails. What's the safest message to show?

screens.heading: Errors that don't snitch
screens.keyPoint: Generic to users, detailed to logs.

screens.body:
Your app probably runs more borrowed code than code you wrote — npm packages, libraries, frameworks. Each one is code you trust blindly.

That trust needs maintenance: run npm audit, keep packages updated, and pin versions so a surprise update can't sneak in.

Before adding a package, glance at its health: recent updates, real maintainers, reasonable download counts. A tiny abandoned package can be the weakest door.

options: To find known vulnerabilities in your dependencies
check.question: Why run npm audit?

screens.heading: Dependencies: borrowed code, your responsibility
screens.keyPoint: Borrowed code is your responsibility — audit and update it.

screens.body:
Logs help you spot attacks and debug incidents — but they're also a treasure chest for attackers: tokens, passwords, and personal data often land there by accident.

Log events, not secrets. Instead of logging a full request, log that it happened — and redact sensitive fields first.

A good test: could you safely show this log line to a stranger? If not, trim it.
screens.heading: Logs are evidence — and targets
screens.keyPoint: Log events, never secrets. Redact first.

screens.body:
Systems fail — the question is which direction they fail. Fail closed means a failure denies access; fail open means a failure grants it.

If your auth check crashes, the safe answer is "no entry", not "come on in". Default-deny is the secure default: start with nothing allowed, then open specific doors.

Apply it everywhere: unknown user → deny. Missing permission → deny. Confusing input → reject, don't guess.

options: Allow access so users aren't blocked
check.question: Your permission check throws an error. Safest behavior?

screens.heading: Fail closed: when in doubt, deny
screens.keyPoint: When in doubt, deny. Default-deny everything.
